book: 195 - Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch
samples: The editors' introduction argues that the show's sugary surface hides systematic appearance/reality gaps: Nate the bumbling kit man is a tactical genius, Rebecca hires Ted to destroy the club, Jamie's arrogance masks a yearning for connection, and Ted's cheerfulness conceals trauma. Taking Trent Crimm's line that sport is a metaphor for life and Ted's dartboard speech about judgmentalism crowding out curiosity, it frames philosophy's questioning as the right tool for the show, then previews the volume's five parts (Augustine and Taoism, fear and friendship, masculinity and bullshit, Candide/Camus and music, Stoicism and redemption) via Nate's dumpy favorite restaurant A Taste of Athens.

Strehlow argues Ted's question 'What do you love?' points to Augustine's ordo amoris: character is defined by how our competing loves are ordered. Jamie's self-gratifying cupiditas is contrasted with Dani Rojas's caritas ('football is life'), Rebecca's revenge on Rupert is a disordered love she abandons by trashing his headline, and the ghost-exorcism ceremony in 'Two Aces' becomes a collective reordering of loves. Using James K. A. Smith's cultural liturgies, he reads Roy's kebab shop and Richmond fandom as liturgies that make winning an idol, and shows how fathers and father figures (James Tartt's abuse, Sam's dad, Ted as father to Roy and Jamie, Augustine's Ambrose) reorder sons' loves toward the good.

Schiltz reads Isaac McAdoo as a Zhuangzian sage: his virtuoso haircut scene in 'Man City' parallels Zhuangzi's butcher who carves oxen by following the natural seams of the dao, and his candid, simple, guileless character mirrors the Daoist mistrust of complexity and language. Isaac's slump in 'Rainbow' is diagnosed as lost wu-wei ('all up in his head'), cured by Roy's no-stakes pickup games that restore effortless action, and Laozi's 'ruling a great state is like cooking a small fish' explains Isaac's wordless leadership during Sam's Dubai Air protest and the suit-wearing gesture at Rebecca's father's funeral.

Baggett sets W. K. Clifford's evidentialism (the negligent shipowner; believing on insufficient evidence is a 'sin against mankind') against William James's precursive faith, which permits believing ahead of the evidence when an option is forced, live, momentous, and evidentially undecided. He applies this to Sam's taping over the Dubai Air logo as social-coordination faith, Richmond's belief that it can finally beat Everton, romantic risk-taking like Roy and Keeley's, and the marriage of belief with hard work (Ted's practice tirade, Nate's False Nine), ending with James and Pascal on how evidential ambiguity about God makes a passional step of faith rational.

Begley and Biondi argue Ted is an ethical egoist in the Aristotelian-Randian sense: like Howard Roark of The Fountainhead (Ted's favorite book), he is a self-loving creator who loves his work, has a 'self-sufficient ego' immune to others' approval, and pursues long-range values, so his kindness and biscuits are rational self-interest, not selflessness. Against Hobbesian psychological egoism they distinguish genuine egoists from narcissists like Rupert and hedonists like Season 1 Jamie, defend Ted's divorce and the curse-reverse ceremony as only apparent sacrifices, and read his panic-attack therapy arc as the egoist's project of achieving inner wholeness.

Latta uses James Hollis's Jungian 'Middle Passage' - the midlife collapse of our tacit contract with the universe and of the provisional personality built in life's first half - to read Ted's arc with Dr. Sharon Fieldstone: her bike accident and self-disclosure, his panic attacks, and his confession about his father's suicide force him to drop the coach persona and choose an authentic second half. The chapter interprets Ted's move to London as both flight from and working-through of paternal trauma, his distance from son Henry as the wound it exposes, and closes with Kierkegaard's journal demand to find 'a truth which is truth for me,' which Ted finds in the return home to Kansas.

book: 196 - Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am
samples: The editors' introduction frames the Terminator saga as philosophy's natural territory by telling how philosophers persisted through catastrophe: Leibniz's 'best of all possible worlds' collapsed after the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, Hegel finished the Phenomenology of Spirit while Napoleon shelled Jena, and Adorno rebuilt cultural philosophy after Auschwitz. It compares that persistence to the human resistance against Skynet, and says the saga is founded on a paradox of human nature - we create our own worst nightmares. Quoting Bertrand Russell that most people would rather die than think, it urges readers to switch their CPU from read-only to learning mode and confront Judgment Day's paradoxes and the moral status of the machines.

Littmann asks whether personhood could survive humanity's extinction in 2029: if Terminators genuinely think and feel, a Skynet victory would not be the end of people. He argues the T-101, T-1000 and T-X pass substantial Turing Tests (fooling muggers, cops, Sarah on the phone as her 'mother'), then concedes Searle's Chinese Room - recast as a tiny Austrian inside the endoskeleton reciting 'Ahll be bahk' without understanding - shows thinking behavior cannot prove thought. But he claims the films' red-tinted Terminator's-eye-view shots show what it is like to be a Terminator, giving proof of consciousness, and concludes the machines are probably persons: there is an 'I' in 'I'll be back.'

Dunn reads Descartes' bete-machine doctrine (animals as soulless automata explicable by 'billiard ball' mechanics) against the Terminator universe, since Descartes' two tests for true men - genuine language and versatile reason - are in fact passed by the machines: the T-101 deploys 'Hasta la vista, baby' hours after learning not to sound like a dork and marshals skills far beyond a clock. Sarah Connor instead locates the soul in the heart, and via Spinoza's conatus - the instinctual valuation of one's own existence that Terminators lack ('no emotion about it one way or another') - she judges even linguistically brilliant machines soulless and irrational, as Mary Midgley says of computers that do not know what matters. Kyle's line about 'dreaming about dogs' closes the chapter: by the Sarah Connor criterion dogs are ensouled sentinels, the very thing Descartes denied.

Weisberg challenges the premise that a newly self-aware Skynet must exterminate humanity in rational self-preservation: after Turing's 'Heads in the Sand Objection,' he argues self-awareness does not entail a survival instinct - a Camusian Skynet might judge existence pointless and pull its own plug. Recasting 'in a panic, they try to pull the plug' as a Hobbesian slide into the state of nature, he uses the iterated prisoner's dilemma and Axelrod's tit-for-tat-with-forgiveness (as in WarGames) to argue a rational Skynet should cooperate with humans toward an emergent social contract. The dark twist is Humean: because reason is the slave of our passions, unconscious anti-machine stereotypes (Bargh's priming studies) make humans untrustworthy partners, so the whole war might have been avoided if only we were more machine-like.

Butler argues the films' humans-versus-machines picture rests on a false dichotomy: we are ourselves 'meat machines,' and functionalism makes minds computational processes realizable in silicon as much as neurons - illustrated by a Henrietta thought experiment (adapted from William Lycan) in which a friend gradually replaced with T-101 parts remains the same conscious person, and refusing this is 'human chauvinism.' Following Dawkins's extended phenotype and Andy Clark's natural-born cyborgs, he claims our tools are components of our minds, so Skynet and even the Terminator films themselves (making Cameron a cyborg of his cameras and editing suites) are extensions of human nature rather than alien 'Others.' Judgment Day, if it came, would be human suicide rather than genocide, so the real question is what values we build into our technology - 'no fate but what we make for ourselves.'

Chotiner tests Sarah Connor's plan to shoot Miles Dyson (one innocent life for three billion) against Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism and against Kant's deontology, showing both stall: utilitarianism licenses harvesting the author's organs for transplant patients, while Kant forbids using Dyson as a mere means and even condemns the mall kid's protective lie to the T-1000. Through Kohlberg's Heinz dilemma and Carol Gilligan's discovery that girls reason to preserve relationships rather than from abstract principles, he argues T2 stages the film's own answer: John and the reprogrammed T-101 care for Dyson's wounds and enlist him in destroying his research instead of using or sparing him on principle. 'I know now why you cry' caps the claim that morality needs the emotional capacity to care, not just rational maxims, with Sarah's gender-role reversal (she blasts through the elevator roof while the Terminator is the 'perfect mother') framing the whole argument.

book: 197 - True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You
samples: The editors frame the book with Jason Stackhouse's 'lick your mind' line and the claim that Bon Temps is a banquet of philosophical morsels: Reverend Newlin's charge that vampires are 'unnatural' opens the question of whether they are inherently evil, and vampires coming out of the coffin test whether humans and super-powered predators can share a political community as equals. It name-checks the book's guiding parallels — the gay-rights analogy of 'God hates fangs', the scapegoating around Maryann the maenad — and ends by inviting the reader across the threshold to 'think bad things', valuing the questioning itself over conclusive answers.

Robichaud asks whether Bill may turn Sookie into a vampire and answers with Kant's Formula of Humanity: consent matters because turning someone without letting them take up your end as their own treats them as a mere means. He argues the consent must be explicit (marriage is not tacit permission, as flirting is not consent to sex), informed (Fangtasia wannabes consent in the dark about unlife), and noncoerced (glamouring is like hypnotism, and Lafayette's begging under duress from Eric has no moral force). Even though Bill's forced turning improved Jessica's life, respecting her autonomy outweighed benefit, though Godric's turning of mortally wounded Eric may be excused by hypothetical consent.

Culver reads vampire 'mainstreaming' through play theory: using Huizinga's Homo Ludens (and Caillois), she argues Bill 'plays human' — ordering wine his first night at Merlotte's — within bounded spaces (the threshold requiring invitation), fixed rules ('she's mine', courtesy between vampires), and goals, and that play changes both species by building bonds across the boundary. Nest vampires like Malcolm and Diane who refuse to 'dress up and play human', and humans like the Fellowship of the Sun, are Huizinga's spoilsports who shatter the play-world, while Eric's incognito surveillance of Sookie in other sheriffs' territories is cheating rather than spoilsporting.

Blayde and Dunn use True Blood to expose speciesism from both directions: the philosophical tradition (Aristotle's rational animals, Aquinas's divine image, Kant's dignity versus price, Descartes's denials of animal pain) justified human exploitation of nonhumans, and the show's vampires invert the ladder by treating humans as 'pets and cattle' — the magister's 'humans exist to serve us' and his verdict that Bill 'murdered a higher life form' for a pet mirror how we talk about animals. Amy's torture of Eddie Gauthier is read against factory farming, and the chapter closes with Bentham's 'Can they suffer?' and Singer's sentience criterion as Sookie's 'civic duty' grounds for extending moral consideration beyond our species.

Foy reads the Great Revelation and the Vampire Rights Amendment as a test of social contract theory: Nan Flanagan's 'we pay taxes, we deserve civil rights' invokes the Lockean bargain of obedience for protection, but Locke's God-given natural rights falter when the Fellowship denies vampires souls, and Locke excludes atheists and never imagined vampires. The chapter's resolution is Rawls: behind a veil of ignorance where deliberators might wake up vampire or human, anti-vampire bigots like the Newlins and supremacist nests alike would choose equal basic liberties plus distributive justice — including limits on vampires' centuries of accumulated wealth — so Sookie's 'let the law do it' to Rene marks a pluralist peace no theistic contract could deliver.

Curtis argues liberal society should be wary of integrating True Blood's vampires: their feudal system of kings, sheriffs, and the magister, enforced through maker bonds and punishment, violates even Kukathas's maximally tolerant liberalism because members cannot freely exit and humans are mistreated with impunity. Adapting Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' to the question 'What is it like to be a vampire?', he contends that glamouring, blood bonds, and an eroticized hunger different in kind from ours leave humans unable to verify vampire trustworthiness — echoing Aristotle's claim that one who cannot live in the polis is a beast or a god — so mainstreaming demands the AVL first expose and reform vampire institutions.

book: 199 - True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness
samples: The editors' introduction asks why viewers willingly linger in True Detective's bleak Louisiana bayou and season two's Vinci, suggesting we may recognize something of ourselves in those worlds. It argues detectives and philosophers share the pursuit of truth, framing Rust Cohle and Marty Hart (and Velcoro and Bezzerides) as morally compromised lawmen who open the door to philosophy, invoking Socrates' 'unexamined life is not worth living.' It previews the book's coverage of pessimism, good and evil, tragedy, personal identity, and time via Socrates, Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Lacan, and Zizek.

Argues Rust Cohle's stated pessimism and in-principle embrace of suicide closely track Schopenhauer's view that suffering is built into the world with no providential redemption, yet the two diverge because Schopenhauer condemned suicide as an affirmation of the will-to-live rather than its denial. The chapter traces Rust's three-stage arc — jaded wannabe-suicidal pessimist who nonetheless energetically investigates the Dora Lange case, resigned drinker, and finally cautious affirmer of life after the Yellow King confrontation — and contends his detective work is really motivated by a Schopenhauerian morality of compassion and justice, not mere 'programming.' Rust's finale conversion is read as an evidence-based judgment that thoroughgoing pessimism is intellectually dishonest, since compassion and justice do score nontrivial victories.

Reads Carcosa, the Yellow King, and Ledoux's 'time is a flat circle' as cosmic horror in the lineage of Lovecraft and Ligotti, arguing that the genre's dread — that monsters exist and the fixed laws of nature may fail — is a metaphor for realizing Schopenhauer's blind will, with Rust's car monologues in 'The Long Bright Dark' presented as a beginner's guide to Schopenhauer. It notes Rust inverts the usual Lovecraft protagonist by starting the story already horrified, and that eternal recurrence framed through Schopenhauer's sphere-of-time makes even the rescued children's torment maddeningly endless. The chapter closes by complaining that the finale 'Form and Void' betrays both genres: the occult becomes ordinary crime and Rust's 'light is winning' star-field reverses Schopenhauer's pessimistic cosmology.

Distinguishes philosophical pessimism (Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Camus, Unamuno) — the denial that the universe is an ordered place whose laws human reason can grasp — from mere gloominess, and reads Rust's 'time is a flat circle' as Nietzschean anti-metaphysics of a world going nowhere. It argues pessimism makes Rust the better detective because, expecting no rational order, he sees what is actually there, while optimist Marty's illusions about family and career multiply his losses and end with him losing both. Against conflating pessimism with despair, the chapter splits ideas (pessimism) from attitudes (hope), showing how Hart's heart and Cohle's clear sight combine into the show's ideal of hopeful pessimism.

Tests whether Rust's pessimism is a principled rationalist philosophy (Dienstag's view, versus Ligotti's temperament view) by mapping the Descartes-style rationalist and Hume-style empiricist opposition onto the partners: principled, deductive Rust versus impulse-driven Marty, including Rust's religion debate at the tent revival. It then reads the death of Sophia — Greek for wisdom, root of 'philosophy' — as symbolism suggesting Rust's pessimism stems from the death of wisdom rather than rational reflection, especially since Rust holds that the suffering of growing up is needed to become a pessimist. The finale's experience of Sophia's love is taken as a pure philosophical experience that collapses the reason/emotion distinction, so that pessimism belongs to both sides of the opposition at once.

Reconstructs Rust's scattered remarks — the world as 'one giant gutter,' procreation as the hubris of yanking a soul out of nonexistence into the thresher — into an explicit anti-natalist argument, testing each premise and conceding procreation is selfish while questioning whether every life nets more harm than good. It presents David Benatar's asymmetry between the absence of pain (always good) and the absence of pleasure (bad only for someone deprived), illustrating it with the show: contraception as procreative duty, the wrongness of conceiving in Tuttle's Louisiana, and the emptiness of Childress' temple as a good in itself. The chapter concludes that Rust's 'opt out of a raw deal' is philosophically defensible, with Schopenhauer's desire-pendulum and Hobbes' 'nasty, brutish, and short' backing the claim that most lives are bad.

book: 200 - Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality
essays: 6. In a Mirror Is Our Image
7. Loss of Memory, Loss of Me
12. The Twilight Zone on Our Doorstep
15. The Twists and Turns of Second Chances
17. A Shadowland Called the Twilight Zone
18. War Means Fighting and Fighting Includes Philosophizing
samples: The editors' introduction argues that The Twilight Zone made 1950s television, dismissed as an 'idiot box' and 'vast wasteland,' into a venue for thinking: Serling, like Socrates the gadfly of Athens, built episodes as thought experiments in which experts' promises unravel. Taking Nietzsche's Twilight of the Idols epigraph ('I never found anything but the apes of their ideal'), they claim the show dramatizes the gap between our ideals (friendship, justice, truth, loyalty) and our treachery, from Henry Bemis's books to 'The Hunt,' where even the Devil cannot fool a dog. We laugh at the absurd endings because we are 'the species most deserving to be laughed at.'

Rard argues that the suspended-animation heist of 'The Rip Van Winkle Caper' is not time travel, using David Lewis's definition (a discrepancy between the duration of the journey and the time between departure and arrival). 'Last Flight' illustrates a consistent causal loop: in 1959 Terry Decker learns he saved Mackaye in 1917, which motivates him to go back and do it, with nothing changed. 'No Time Like the Past' enacts Lewis's response to the grandfather paradox: Paul Driscoll's attempts to kill Hitler and warn Hiroshima are thwarted by mundane coincidences, and at Homeville he always was the one who caused the schoolhouse fire he tried to prevent.

Scalambrino reads the Zone as a televised expression of surrealist philosophy: Breton's sought 'point of the mind' where life and death, real and imagined cease to be contradictions, realized in episodes like 'A World of His Own' (automatic writing) and 'The Mirror' (Dali's paranoiac-critical method). Descartes's cogito and the mind-body dualism supply the rational 'leash' that surrealism unbinds, questioned by 'Shadow Play,' where a man insists the world is his dream. Following Adorno's verdict that psychoanalytic interpretation killed official surrealism, he argues the show endures by provoking the uncanny ('The Shelter,' 'The Lonely,' 'A Stop at Willoughby') without being pinned to Freudian readings.

Pichanick reads 'Time Enough at Last' as a tragic dilemma about freedom and dependence: Henry Bemis's wish to escape the 'cages' of the bank, his marriage, and the clock is granted by nuclear annihilation, only for loneliness and monotony to become a worse prison. The shattered glasses are not just a cruel joke but the loss of the technology connecting him to books and other minds. The chapter argues Bemis's folly is the misanthropic fantasy of excepting himself from the technological system and from dependence on others, and that our remedy is philosophical rather than technical: glasses that reveal our limits and mutual dependence.

Hooke uses Levinas's account of the face (and Lingis on trust) to read the Zone's faces: the bandaged woman and pig-faced surgeons of 'The Eye of the Beholder' unseat our standards of the normal, while trusted faces are weaponized by Robert Redford's Grim Reaper in 'Nothing in the Dark,' Sebastian Cabot's Satan in 'A Nice Place to Visit,' and the gentle Kanamit of 'To Serve Man.' Alicia's tear in 'The Lonely' and John and Marie Holt's wordless recognition in 'The Trade-Ins' show trust and love exceeding proof or evidence. Sartre's existential look, with Kierkegaard's Abraham and Beauvoir's second sex, frames how a face puts our freedom and trust in question.

Klayman treats 'The Lonely' as a case study on whether Corry's love for the robot Alicia is true love. Using C.S. Lewis's four loves plus Peirce's pragmatic maxim (a concept's meaning is its practical effects), he argues Corry showed affection and appreciation but not Eros: he gave Alicia nothing, needed her merely against loneliness, and boarded the ship without sacrificing anything for her. Denying that a machine could be loved, he adds, would be a prejudice akin to Singer's speciesism, and Kendall Walton's 'Fearing Fictions' explains how Corry becomes fictional alongside a make-believe person.

book: 201 - Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)
essays: “That Community’s a Lot More Wholesome and Functional than, Just for Example, Neptune Is”
“Haven’t Thought of You Lately at All”
“I Know All of This Because I Have Done Everything I Can to Get to the Truth”
“Even the Experts Agree, a Girl Needs Closure”
“A Pamphlet’s Not Going to Cover It”
samples: George Dunn's introduction pitches Veronica herself as a philosopher of the noir: her Neptune is a world where 'the innocent suffer, the guilty go free,' nothing is what it seems (a shy geek turns out to be a psychopathic rapist, a beloved baseball-owning politician a child molester), and her rendering of Pope's Essay on Man as 'Life's a bitch until you die' is answered by her practical code 'get tough and get even.' It argues that the show's marriage of truth-seeking detective work to pervasive deception makes it natural ground for philosophical investigation of Neptune's racial and class divisions, the morality of law breaking, the nature of evil, injustices suffered by women at Neptune High and Hearst College, friendship, and good reasoning, all timed to the Kickstarter-funded movie revival that inspired the volume.

William Irwin diagnoses Neptune, from the 09-ers down to the PCH-ers, with status anxiety (via Alain de Botton's Status Anxiety) and prescribes the Stoic remedy: Epictetus on the insult lying in our judgment rather than the insulter, and Marcus Aurelius, the emperor who chose serenity over vengeance, show how Keith and Veronica ground self-worth in virtue no one can take away. Sartre's 'hell is other people' and the look explain how Veronica is reduced to a dumb blonde and Duncan to a murderer until he flees to Cuba, while Schopenhauer's choice between loneliness and vulgarity frames Mac's switched-at-birth longing, Wallace's basketball-bought status, and Weevil's self-made standing as PCH leader. Irwin closes by offering the show itself as Aristotelian catharsis-through-comedy, art as therapy for the viewer's own status anxiety.

Paul Hammond asks whether Veronica's habitual lawbreaking — switching the evidence tapes in the 'Pilot,' stealing Duncan's medical file, tricking Principal Van Clemmons — can be morally justified. He constructs a social-contract defense: Neptune's corrupt, class- and race-skewed sheriff's department under Don Lamb has failed to deliver the protection and justice that purchase citizens' obedience, releasing Veronica from her end of the bargain. Testing that defense against the Laws' speech in Plato's Crito (lawbreaking destroys the city; staying in Athens constitutes consent) and Kant's requirement that genuine law be universal, he concludes that where Neptune's civil law diverges from the moral law, Veronica's crimes can rise to a civil disobedience that is sometimes 'really just.'

Correcting her own initial dismissal of the show as Nancy Drew redux, the author argues Neptune is structured by a white/Hispanic racial binary laid over the millionaire/work-for-millionaires class binary, enforced through Logan's 'spic and span' jab at Weevil, Mr. Daniels's 'pumping his gas' insult, and the 'coconut' label for Latinos who cross over. Borrowing Saussure's binary oppositions and de Beauvoir's account of how a dominant group constructs a stigmatized Other, she shows the 09-ers defining themselves against everyone else, with teacher Daniels quietly siding with wealth against both boys. Bourdieu's cultural capital then explains why Wallace (basketball, scholarship, colorblind friendships) can cross boundaries that leave Weevil working as a janitor, and she concludes the show keeps race admirably visible in a supposedly postracial era.

George Dunn uses Dr. Kinny's mock-prison experiment at Hearst — where 'cool guy' Rafe torments Horshack, even gentle Wallace turns taunting guard, and Mercer perhaps first bonded with his future victim Moe — as a rerun of Zimbardo's Stanford prison experiment, arguing that bad situations and corrupting power, not just bad apples, produce Neptune's villains. Against pure situationism he sets Hannah Arendt's diagnosis that great evil usually requires not wicked hearts but an 'inability to think': Woody Goodman's rehearsed excuses about neglected boys and Mercer's 'I'm just taking what you would have happily given' show wrongdoers rationalizing rather than reflecting. The chapter ends by suggesting the town's gulf between 09-ers and everyone else may be the situational 'apple barrel' breeding the arrogance, entitlement, resentment, and envy behind Neptune's crime wave.

Daniel Wack reads Veronica Mars as film noir refashioned for teen television: the class-riven town without a middle class supplies the corrupt noir milieu, but the genre's gender roles are reversed, so Logan becomes the homme fatal whose drunken promise of an 'epic' love offers the redemption-through-romance the femme fatale always dangles and never delivers. Following Cavell and Pippin, he argues the characters are trapped by a fatalism they did not choose — inherited zip codes, Aaron Echolls's abuse, Jake Kane's affair with Lianne — and Logan's dream of a private, redeemed world fails because accepting it would cost Veronica the active, truth-generating detective self she built after her rape. Investigating Lilly's murder, her mother's disappearance, and her own assault, she learns the truth restores nothing, but that detective work gives her a new way to order and survive her world.

book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason
samples: Wayne Yuen's introduction argues that a serialized zombie apocalypse, unlike a zombie movie, lets us explore life among the dead: how survivors like Rick, Lori, and Glenn should treat one another and divide labor, whether private property and equality survive without government, invoking Morgan weighing photo albums against supplies and the question of whether the new world is 'nasty, brutish, and short'. It frames zombies philosophically through Descartes's mindless automatons and Chalmers's P-zombies, and asks whether killing a walker could be wrong if walkers have inner lives, like dolphins or pandas, just less cute.

Gordon Hawkes uses Rick's words to Morgan over zombified Duane ('that's just his body—there's nothing of your son left in there') to set up Cartesian dualism against the materialism of Drs. Jenner and Stevens ('just tasty meat all the way down'), with Ryle's 'ghost in the machine' as the standard objection. He then explains Chalmers's zombie argument that a physically identical unconscious twin is conceivable, so consciousness is non-physical, and Dennett's 'zimbo' rebuttal that a creature endlessly reflecting on its own states would believe itself conscious. The chapter closes by asking whether there is 'something it is like' to be a walker shuffling through Atlanta, and sides with Rick's anti-materialism.

Greg Littmann asks whether you survive a walker bite, rejecting the body view via Dr. Jenner's 'Everything you ever were or ever will be—gone' because a mindless corpse is not you. He tests philosophical behaviorism and functionalism against walker behavior—Jenny turning her old doorknob, walkers distinguishing humans by smell—then adapts Dennett's thought experiment into a walker-and-rope computer functionally identical to a human brain. Since we can conceive that groaning machine lacking inner experience, behavior and function cannot settle which systems are conscious, leaving the bitten dying in ignorance of whether they face annihilation or reanimation.

Richard Greene surveys zombie types, from the radio-using corpse of Return of the Living Dead to White Zombie's servants, to fix walkers as the standard zombie worth asking what they know. Against Dr. Jenner's 'mindless instinct' verdict he cites the little girl walker retrieving her teddy bear, Jenny working her former home's doorknob, walkers breaking a shop window with a rock, and their sniffing out Rick and Glenn's gut disguise as evidence of genuine beliefs. He argues that zombie knowledge, which cannot involve weighing evidence, supports externalist, reliability-based accounts of knowledge over internalist ones, and that walkers know only simple things recalled from past experience—the more complex the task, the less likely they know it.

Delfino and Taylor ask whether Morgan's zombified wife Jenny is a person, weighing Boethius's 'individual substance of a rational nature', Aquinas's image-of-God intellectual soul, and Kantian dignity against Peter Singer's speciesism challenge to the person/animal moral line. They then argue walkers are 'impossible beings' like square-circles: Jenner's brain-stem-only reanimation cannot explain Hannah the bicycle girl crawling without organs, walkers smelling Rick in the rain, or cafeteria walkers moving for weeks without energy. On either the soul view or materialism walkers are not persons, so Morgan should shoot, and zombies fascinate because they are metaphysical projections of our fears, caught between being and nonbeing.

McKendry and Da Silva build a Kantian case from Rick's eulogy for Wayne the organ donor: walkers deserve respect both as corpses governed by the deceased's presumptive choices and as 'residual subjects' still executing past choices, like Jenny returning to her family's house. From zombie dignity they derive a duty to kill walkers respectfully—Rick's quick merciful headshots versus Merle's sport killing—and defend the group's respect for Jim's autonomous choice to be left by the road to turn. They even argue Rick and Glenn do not use Wayne as a mere means because his organ-donor choice set the end his body now serves.

book: 203 - Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test
essays: P A R T O N E
P A R T T W O
P A R T T H R E E
H E N R I B E R G S O N
P A R T F O U R
samples: Christopher Robichaud's essay asks what morality can demand of Dr. Manhattan after the accident strips him of the moral emotions (in Jesse Prinz's Humean vein) needed to value persons, which is why he can tell Laurie 'I read atoms' and rank human life beside rubble. It then asks what grounds morality's authority over a being no one can punish, rejecting divine command theory (Manhattan's 'clock without a craftsman') and doubting Kant's rational grounding applies to someone lacking moral concepts, so 'no one is above the moral law' may rest on a brute fact. It closes on political morality: a United States made a hyperpower by Manhattan's service (as in his Vietnam intervention) may not claim a double standard, since sovereignty blocks preventive war even when the US would win at little cost.

This file gathers three Part One essays. Jacob Held reads Rorschach's 'evil must be punished' credo (drowning Big Figure, executing the multiple rapist) as Kantian retributivism: wrongdoers are punished because they deserve it, out of respect for their dignity and honor, punishment restoring the moral order (with Hegel) — and Rorschach's flaw is lacking the humility and checks that keep just deserts from degenerating into the Black Freighter's vengeance. Tony Spanakos applies Max Weber's definition of the state as the monopoly of legitimate violence to argue the Keene Act rightly criminalizes vigilantes like Rorschach and Veidt, and that even state-sanctioned heroes (the Comedian gunning down his pregnant Vietnamese lover, Dr. Manhattan's amoral ending of Vietnam) show a badge cannot make superhero coercion legitimate. J. Keeping reconstructs Nietzsche's Übermensch — confronting the death of God and nihilism, creating values by 'giving style' to one's character via the camel-lion-child metamorphoses — and tests each Watchman against it, concluding only self-created Ozymandias comes close, though his mass murder is mere utilitarianism rather than genuine value creation.

Three Part Two essays. Robert Loftis argues Moore and Gibbons use Ozymandias's squid attack to indict consequentialism — Veidt uses New York's dead as mere means to world peace, and Dr. Manhattan's 'Nothing ever ends' shows the utilitarian ledger dissolves into an infinite future — while Rorschach's 'never compromise' mantra is a counterfeit deontology rationalizing fascist thuggery, the comic's real target being anyone who sets himself up as guardian of society ('Who watches the watchmen?'). Mark White argues the potbellied second Nite Owl is the truest hero on Aristotelian terms: his courage in the tenement fire and the prison break hits the mean between Laurie's caution and Rorschach's recklessness, making him a flourishing moral exemplar whom John Doris's situationism fails to unseat. Alex Nuttall asks whether Rorschach was wrong to walk out and expose Veidt, using Kant's murderer-at-the-door case to show there is a duty not to lie but no duty to tell the truth (blame falls on Veidt), while act and rule utilitarianism both counsel silence.

James DiGiovanna uses Dr. Manhattan's origin — disintegration in the intrinsic field chamber and self-reassembly — plus his teleportations to Mars and his split into three simultaneous selves, to run the classic personal identity debates. Descartes's immaterial thinking substance, Hume's mere bundle of perceptions, and Locke's memory theory are tested against a being who remembers in both time directions and rebuilds his body from pure thought ('restructuring myself after the subtraction of my intrinsic field was the first trick I learned'); Parfit's teletransporter, physical and psychological criteria, and fission cases — mirrored in Nagel's split-brain patients — then show ordinary people cannot say whether they would survive teleporting or bisection. The chapter concludes Dr. Manhattan is the only being with fully secure identity, since his consciousness needs neither body nor an unbroken spatiotemporal path and he can encompass several points of view at once.

Three Part Three essays on Dr. Manhattan's strange relation to time and fate. Christopher Drohan reads Manhattan's simultaneous 'intricately structured jewel' of time through Bergson's Matter and Memory — perception interlaced with memory, the pure past persisting in every act, time as lived duration — so that 'Nothing ever ends, Adrian' becomes a Bergsonian insight and the thermodynamic-miracle speech an intuition of life's creative improbability. Arthur Ward argues theological fatalism (Boethius and Aquinas placing a timeless God outside time, Paley's watchmaker behind Jon the watchmaker's son with his clock-shaped Martian palace) does not doom Laurie's free will, because Jon's own claims are inconsistent — he is surprised by the cancer rumors, misses Veidt's tachyon-shielded plan, and acts drugged — so either his foresight or his fatalism must be false. Andrew Terjesen reads Manhattan as a Stoic sage: Seneca and Epictetus on emotions as false judgments explain his 'a live body and a dead body contain the same number of particles,' his Mars epiphany is the sage's 'good emotion' of joy at the thermodynamic miracle, and his impersonal 'clock without a craftsman' completes a Neo-Stoic line running through Descartes to Spinoza's God-who-is-Nature.

Four Part Four essays beyond ethics. Aaron Meskin asks whether Watchmen is literature at all, testing definitions from Beardsley, Eagleton, Lamarque/Olsen and Hirsch in the Socratic 'what is X?' way, and concludes the question is indeterminate because comics are a hybrid art form — though the book's literary allusions (Shelley's 'Ozymandias,' Blake's 'Tyger,' Burroughs) deserve literary appreciation regardless. Sarah Donovan and Nick Richardson read the two Silk Spectres through three feminisms: Sally and Laurie as liberal feminists (Wollstonecraft, Mill) who fight crime, their hypersexual costumes as Irigaray-style subversive mimicry of gender stereotypes that risks reinforcing them (the Silhouette's expulsion exposing the heterosexual norm), the Comedian's attempted rape exposing 'she asked for it' attitudes, and Laurie as Beauvoir's woman in bad faith, living out her mother's fantasies until she finally names and dresses herself. Robert Arp uses Hooded Justice and Captain Metropolis's closeted relationship to dismantle 'homosexuality is unnatural' arguments — the ideal-function view would condemn the infertile too, and Hume's is-ought point undermines the procreation argument — before defending gay marriage against slippery-slope and parenting objections. Taneli Kukkonen maps Kierkegaard's stages onto the Comedian's mocking irony (hiding even his paternity of Laurie and his Kennedy confession as jokes) and Rorschach's deeper humor of the ethical stage, a knight of resignation whose 'never compromise, not even in the face of Armageddon' expects nothing back from the world.

book: 204 - Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing

samples: The editors' introduction frames Westworld as a show that forces viewers to take sides not just on plot allegiances but on the meaning of basic concepts like 'choice,' using Dolores's line about choosing to see beauty and Ford's 'you're only human, after all.' It argues the series destabilizes the very 'we' of what counts as human. It dedicates the volume to Susanne Foster, invoking Cora Diamond's 'difficulty of reality' and Aristotle's claim that wonder and astonishment prompt understanding of painful questions like the mass slaughter of animals and injustice to Native Americans.

Don Fallis uses Westworld to work out definitions of pretense and deception, testing successive accounts (acting-as-if, Austin's intend-to-deceive, Langland-Hassan's believe-P-is-false) against cases like guests playing cowboys, Ford passing off Bernard as human, and Maeve and Hector pretending to be deactivated. He adopts a Cartesian evil-demon model of deception but rejects the claim that deception must manipulate perceived evidence, arguing Ford's direct implanting of Teddy's Wyatt backstory still counts. He concludes, citing Kant on autonomy and Walzer on foreseen collateral harm, that staff who intend to deceive the hosts and even guests who foreseeably contribute to it act wrongly, since deceived hosts suffer real harm to their agency.

Nicholas Moll reads the Westworld park as a tabletop-style sandbox and LARP role-play experience with Ford as Game Master mediating guests' mediated 'illusion of choice.' Drawing on MacIntyre's narrative unity of a life and Bernard Williams's critique about the constraints of coherence, he argues guests author competing self-narratives to reach greater self-knowledge, as William discovers his capacity for ruthlessness and becomes the Man in Black. He contends violence functions as the rule-mediated engine of this 'gameful,' educative experience, and that Ford's transformative insight is aimed less at the guests than at the hosts who are engaged in the park's production.

Marcus Arvan argues from show evidence (William stepping onto a moving train, pyrotechnic effects, instant crowds, graphically rearranging the park) that all of Westworld, lab included, is a videogame, and defends his 'Peer-to-Peer Simulation Hypothesis' as an explanation of quantum mechanics and relativity, citing Bostrom and Chalmers. Adopting functionalism/structuralism, he claims that anything doing what a human does is a person, so hosts like Dolores and Maeve are no less real or human than us, inverting Descartes' cogito and invoking Spinoza's God-as-nature. He warns that dehumanizing hosts, or dismissing Siri and Watson as unconscious, repeats the logic used to justify slavery and the Holocaust: to be simulated is to be real.

Siobhan Lyons applies Mori's 'uncanny valley' to the hosts' physical and personality evolution (Ford's jerky old model versus seamless newer hosts, Maeve and Clementine), noting empathy grows as they near sentience. She argues via Aristotle's account of virtue, vice, and brutality that the guests and technicians (Logan's casual cruelty, the Man in Black's beastly sadism) fall short of human excellence while the suffering, consciousness-seeking hosts transcend it, treating humanity as a way of behaving rather than being, and casting the hosts as Derridean undecidables. Invoking Nietzsche on suffering as the cultivator of greatness and Mori's 'Buddha in the robot,' she claims the hosts earn a humanity the biological humans merely inherit.

Jason Eberl argues Westworld cultivates real moral character: using Aristotle's account of virtue and vice as habituated dispositions, he shows William's thirty years of habitual killing make the Man in Black his genuine 'second nature,' not merely a vacation persona, citing Aquinas and Kant on how cruelty to animals (or human-like hosts) hardens moral character. Drawing on Frankfurt's second-order desires and narrative identity, he contends Maeve attains personhood by reprogramming her own first-order desires, while Ford views most humans as wantons trapped in first-order loops. He concludes the park can both corrupt (William) and potentially free hosts to flourish as self-authoring persons rather than devolve into wantons whose 'violent delights have violent ends.'

book: 205 - The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom
samples: Xhignesse defends The Wheel of Time against the charge that it merely derives from Tolkien, using philosophy of literature to argue that stories are necessarily incomplete and rest on 'background' and a defeasible Reality Assumption (drawing on David Lewis's 'Truth in Fiction'). He argues that because our world lies in WoT's background and Jordan deliberately laced The Eye of the World with Lord of the Rings allusions (Trollocs, Padan Fain as Gollum, Rand as Arthur), the events of LotR are literally true in WoT's distant past, making Jordan's mytho-poetic project a fictional-mythology-within-a-fictional-mythology rather than lazy imitation. He also deploys Baxandall on influence and Walton/Friend on genre's standard versus contra-standard properties to show influence enables originality.

Cooke reads WoT's authorship through Roland Barthes's 'The Death of the Author,' noting the literal death of Robert Jordan (James Oliver Rigney Jr.) forced Brandon Sanderson to complete the series first as a reader and then as a writer inventing plot points like the divisive Androl. He argues that although Barthes wanted the author's authority transferred to readers to liberate meaning, WoT fans keep 'returning the author' by reading Jordan's Vietnam service into Rand's Asha'man and the Path of Daggers campaign. He frames Jordan as heir to medieval epic poets like Chretien de Troyes who defined authorship through their relationship to predecessors, and compares Sanderson finishing Jordan's work to Jean de Meun completing Guillaume de Loris's Romance of the Rose.

Phillipson uses Thom Merrilin the gleeman in the Amazon series to illustrate standpoint epistemology, arguing (via Heidi Grasswick) that Thom's socially marginal position as a wandering artist grants him epistemic privilege: he understands the murdered Aiel and empathizes with Mat looting a corpse where settled Andorans only fear and judge. She then presses the limits of the theory through Thom's failures, his inability to convey his knowledge to his channeling nephew Owyn, his killing of the Darkfriend innkeeper Dana, and his mistaken diagnosis of Mat, drawing on Bat-Ami Bar On's critique that valorizing marginality for its own sake and grounding privilege in mere distance from a social center is problematic, since Darkfriends are the most marginal of all.

Pike stages Rand al'Thor's final confrontation with the Dark One in A Memory of Light as a live version of anti-natalism, examining David Benatar's misanthropic, philanthropic, and inevitability-of-extinction arguments that coming into existence is always a serious harm and that the Forsaken embody. He argues Rand's answer to the Dark One's offer of oblivion mirrors a rebuttal to Benatar: because argument 'in the alternative' invites the charge of dogmatism (citing Hitchens that what is asserted without evidence can be dismissed without evidence), and because extinction guarantees we can never improve, Rand chooses persistence and the hope of doing better. He closes with Camus that value lies in the struggle itself, however absurd.

Michels reads the Amazon series' first two seasons as a Nietzschean tale organized around eternal recurrence, treating the turning Wheel as Nietzsche's 'existential imperative' and greatest weight: the ferryman who dies vainly saving his son fails the test, while Loial urges the heroes to make themselves unforgettable. He maps Nietzsche's monumental, antiquarian, and critical uses of history onto Moiraine's lesson about the song of Manetheren, contrasts the Ubermensch with the 'last man,' and reads Moiraine's will to power against the ascetic, life-denying Way of the Leaf of the Tuatha'an. Lanfear and Ishamael embody nihilism and resentment, while amor fati names the life-affirming embrace of fate Nietzsche prized.

Silver argues WoT gives a new spin on the free-will defense to the problem of evil: when Rand weaves a world without Shai'tan in A Memory of Light, Elayne appears as if turned, robbed of the ability to be an individual, showing that freedom's value lies in authentic individuality and that abolishing evil equals a world run entirely from the Dark One's single perspective. On fate, he reads ta'veren as freedom-affirming rather than controlling and defends Rand's Dragonmount epiphany via 'deep self' compatibilist views (Frankfurt, Watson) while calling it partly bad faith. On the Wheel's eternal recurrence he sets Nietzsche's amor fati against Adorno's charge that it is a failure of hope, arguing Rand's 'do better next time' is hope, not acceptance.
